title: Scotch Broth
subtitle: Lamb neck, pearl barley, and root vegetables in a clear broth
excerpt: Scotch broth is a deep, nourishing Scottish soup built on lamb neck and pearl barley with root vegetables and kale. The neck gives the broth its body and the pearl barley thickens it slowly as it cooks. It is a whole meal in a bowl, and it improves significantly the day after it is made.
sourceNotes: Scotch broth has been recorded in Scottish cooking since at least the seventeenth century. The combination of mutton or lamb, pearl barley, and turnip or swede in a clear broth is the standard form. Kale is a traditional addition in colder months.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large pot and freeze half. The flavour improves each time it is reheated.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make 1 to 2 days ahead for best flavour. Refrigerate and skim any fat from the surface before reheating.

glossaryTerms.definition: Barley grains with the husk removed and the outer bran layer polished off. They cook relatively quickly and swell to release starch, thickening the liquid they cook in.

content.text: Scotch broth takes time but not attention. Lamb neck goes into cold water and simmers for an hour before the vegetables and barley are added. This first stage draws the body and flavour from the bone. The
absorbs the broth as it cooks and makes the soup thicker and more filling as it sits. Skim the surface in the first 15 minutes to remove any grey foam from the meat.

items.prepNote: bone-in neck chops or neck fillet

content.text: Put the lamb neck in a large pot and cover with 2 litres of cold water. Bring to a simmer over medium heat. Skim off any grey foam that rises in the first 10 to 15 minutes. Add the bay leaves and thyme. Simmer gently for 1 hour until the lamb is just tender.

Lift out the lamb. Add the rinsed pearl barley, {{onion}} chopped onion, {{leek}} sliced leek, {{carrot}} diced carrot, {{swede}} diced swede, and {{celery}} sliced celery to the broth. Simmer for 40 minutes.

When the lamb is cool enough to handle, pull the meat from the bones and shred it roughly. Discard the bones and any sinew. Return the meat to the soup. If using kale, add it now and cook for 10 minutes.
Taste and season generously with salt and pepper. Remove the bay leaves and thyme stems. Stir in the parsley. Serve in deep bowls with crusty bread.

items.cause: The lamb boiled rather than simmered, or the foam was not skimmed.
items.fix: Maintain a gentle simmer throughout , the surface should barely ripple. Skim all grey foam in the first 15 minutes.

items.symptom: The barley has absorbed all the liquid and the soup is very thick
items.cause: The barley was added too early or the soup was simmered uncovered.
items.fix: Add the barley after the initial hour. It will thicken the soup as it sits , add more hot water if needed to reach the consistency you want.

items.cause: It was not cooked long enough. Neck needs time to soften.
items.fix: Simmer for the full hour at minimum. When the lamb pulls easily from the bone, it is done.

items.cause: Insufficient salt, or the lamb stock was weak.
items.fix: Season generously at the end after the full cooking time. The barley absorbs salt, so the soup will need more than seems right mid-way through cooking.

content.text: Scotch broth is the national soup of Scotland in the same way that borsch is Russian or minestrone is Italian: deeply regional, completely identified with its place, and made in a thousand slightly different versions by as many home cooks. The pearl barley is the ingredient that distinguishes it from a plain lamb broth, and the swede is the root vegetable that defines it as distinctly northern. Make a large pot on a Sunday and eat from it for three days.
